title: World Cup 2026: Everything You Need to Know About the Biggest Tournament in History
summary: The FIFA World Cup expands to 48 teams and three host nations for the first time. We break down the format, the favourites, and why this edition could be the most dramatic yet.
content:
The 2026 FIFA World Cup is unlike any that has come before it. For the first time in the tournament's history, three nations share hosting duties — the United States, Canada, and Mexico — across 16 cities and 11 stadiums. The competition has grown from 32 to 48 teams, adding a third group-stage match and a new round of 16 to the knockout structure. And it arrives in North America at a moment when football's popularity on the continent has never been higher.

It is the biggest World Cup in history. And the expectation is that it will produce the best one.

The Expanded Format

Sixteen additional teams means 16 additional nations in the greatest football competition on earth. For continental associations that have historically been underrepresented — CONCACAF, CAF, AFC — the expansion delivers more guaranteed places and more opportunities for upsets.

The 48-team format divides into 12 groups of four, with the top two teams from each group plus the eight best third-placed sides progressing to a round of 32. Critics worried that the expansion would dilute quality and produce meaningless dead rubbers. The counter-argument — that the first round's upsets are what make World Cups memorable — has proved more persuasive to FIFA's leadership.

The Favourites

France remain the benchmark. Kylian Mbappé, now in his late 20s and playing the best football of his career, leads a generation of players who grew up watching the 2018 triumph and are desperate to add a second star to the shirt. The squad is deeper than it was eight years ago, the defensive structure more reliable, and the manager — whoever FIFA's draw places against them — will face a team with no obvious weakness.

Brazil have rebuilt after years of underachievement. Argentina arrive as defending champions, with Lionel Messi in what will almost certainly be his final World Cup. England, Germany, Spain, and Portugal all have legitimate claims to contention.

This is the year we bring it home. I have never felt more ready, and I have never been part of a squad with this quality and this hunger. We are not coming to participate. We are coming to win. — Kylian Mbappé

The Host Nations

All three host nations qualify automatically — a decision that generated debate, particularly regarding Canada and the United States, whose football development is genuine but whose historical standing in the game is modest compared to traditional powers. The United States, however, have consistently improved under their current coaching staff and will arrive at the tournament as a team with a realistic chance of reaching the knockout rounds on merit.

Mexico, with their historically consistent World Cup record and passionate football culture, are a genuine dark horse. And playing in front of their own supporters — in stadiums that will be overwhelmingly Mexican in terms of atmosphere — represents a significant advantage in the group stage.

The Stadiums

The venues span a continent: MetLife Stadium in New York, the Rose Bowl in Los Angeles, Estadio Azteca in Mexico City, and BC Place in Vancouver among others. Each city brings a different atmosphere, a different climate, a different football culture. The logistics of competing across a tournament spread over three countries will test every squad's planning and adaptability.

The final is scheduled for MetLife Stadium in New Jersey — the largest stadium in the tournament, capable of holding over 82,000 supporters. It will be the most watched sporting event in human history.
